description: The `common` resolver tier: the assets nearly every charter references. It ships with the client and is cached, so the ordinary charter compiles with no round trip (spec §2.10.7). This file is a fixture for the conformance corpus — a real deployment's resolver is a service, and this is the shape it serves.
notes: `issuer` comes from curation and never from on-chain metadata (S10). Token metadata is self-asserted, so an issuer copied from it is worthless as a discriminator — and the issuer segment is what separates native from bridged.
`decimals` is the sole authority for money conversion (§2.6). More than nine makes an asset unusable (E223).
A `common` entry must be identical to the `full` entry for the same mint (S13); where they disagree, both fail closed for that mint.

mints.note: Bridged. Same symbol as Circle's and a different issuer, which is why the issuer segment is the equivalence key for an asset group (S22): this is a different credit risk that happens to share a ticker.
Nine decimals is the cap (§2.6), so this is the widest scale the language accepts.
Eighteen decimals, so E223 refuses it. Present deliberately: the resolver knows the asset and the language declines to bound it, which is the honest outcome rather than a lookup failure.
Revoked. A revoked mint always stops the charters that name it (E406): revocation is the mechanism for "this turned out to be something else", so it must not be absorbed quietly.
Devnet. The genesis identity differs, so a devnet charter fails S7 on mainnet and vice versa — which is what makes rehearsal structurally safe rather than merely conventional.

units.note: A unit:// limit must declare a rate source and a staleness bound and must deny when the rate is stale (S11). No source is listed here, so a charter using it for a non-USD payment fails E404 rather than assuming 1:1.
